title: 7 Early Signs of Wood Rot on Your Deck
description: Spongy boards, dark rings at fasteners, and soft joist tops show up long before a deck board breaks. Learn the 7 early signs of deck rot and how to stop it.
excerpt: Seven early warning signs of deck rot, how to probe for it, and what to repair before the next stain coat goes on.
h1: 7 Early Signs of Wood Rot on Your Deck (Before It Fails)
heroIntro: Deck boards rarely fail without warning. Decay fungi need weeks or months of sustained moisture, and they leave clues along the way. Here is how to find them while the fix is still a few boards and not a rebuild.

keywords.primary: signs of wood rot on deck
secondary: how to tell if deck is rotting
questions: How can you tell if a deck board is rotting?
Can you stain over rotted deck wood?
How do you stop deck wood from rotting in Florida?

sections.h2: Why decks rot from the bottom up
body: Wood decay fungi become active when the moisture content of the wood stays above roughly 20 percent for an extended period. On a Florida deck, the tops of the boards dry quickly in the sun, but the undersides, the joist tops beneath them, and the end grain stay damp for days after a storm. That is why deck rot usually starts underneath, where you are not looking, and works its way up.

Pressure-treated lumber resists decay, but it is not immune. Cut ends and drilled holes expose untreated wood at the core, and boards rated for above-ground use will break down faster if they are kept wet by debris, poor drainage, or close contact with soil.

bullets: Spongy or bouncy spots underfoot, especially near the house, steps, or under planters.
Dark rings around fasteners: black or rust-colored staining spreading out from screws and nails, which signals water wicking into the hole.
Checks and splits that stay dark long after the rest of the board has dried.
Fibers that break short across the grain instead of splintering long when you pry with an awl.
Cupped or sagging boards, or fasteners that have backed out because the wood around them softened.
Fungal growth, white or brown threads, or small mushroom-like bodies on the underside or at the ledger.
Soft joist tops or a ledger board with stains running down the house wall below it.

sections.h2: How to inspect your deck in 30 minutes
body: Bring a flashlight, an awl or flat screwdriver, and a pencil. Probe the boards around posts, stair stringers, and any spot where water collects. Healthy wood resists and splinters; decayed wood lets the tip sink in and breaks off in short, crumbly pieces. Then get underneath if the deck height allows, and probe the tops of joists, the beam, the post bases, and the ledger where the deck attaches to the house. Circle every soft spot with the pencil so you can count them.

Pay special attention to the ledger. A rotted ledger or missing flashing over it is a structural safety issue, not a cosmetic one. If you find softness there, at post bases, or in the joists, stop using that section and have it assessed by a qualified deck contractor before anyone refinishes it.

An inexpensive pin-type moisture meter takes the guesswork out of deck maintenance. Take readings on a few boards in the sun, a few in the shade, and on the joist tops if you can reach them. Wood that reads consistently high days after the last rain is wood that is not drying, and that is where decay will start. Readings are also how you decide when it is safe to stain: most penetrating stain manufacturers specify a maximum moisture content, and applying over wet wood leads to blotchy color, poor penetration, and early failure.

In our area, the best windows for deck work are usually the drier months from fall through spring. During the summer rainy season, it can take a run of storm-free days for boards to dry enough, and mornings often start damp even when afternoons are hot.
Stain will not fix rotted wood, and it can hide it for another season. Repairs come first.
bullets: Replace any deck board that gives under the probe. Patching a decayed board with filler on a walking surface does not hold.
Treat every fresh cut end of pressure-treated lumber with an end-cut wood preservative before installing it.
Have damaged joists, beams, posts, or ledger sections repaired by a deck builder; this is structural carpentry.
Clean the whole deck with a deck cleaner and a gentle rinse; avoid high pressure, which raises the grain and chews up soft earlywood.
Let the wood dry until it reads below the stain manufacturer’s moisture limit, usually a few dry days in a row.
Apply a penetrating stain that soaks into the wood rather than a film-forming paint that can trap moisture and peel.

sections.h2: Prevention that works in our climate
body: Think about where water goes after a storm. If it has to sit, the wood will eventually pay for it. A deck built tight to the ground with no airflow, boards laid without gaps, and a ledger without flashing are all set up to stay wet; some of those can only be fixed by a builder, but the routine habits below help every deck.

Moisture control is everything. Sweep leaves and pine needles out of board gaps so water drains, keep gutter downspouts from dumping onto the deck, and move planters onto risers. Make sure soil and mulch stay clear of the framing. Most importantly, keep the wood protected with a penetrating deck stain on a regular schedule. In full Florida sun, horizontal surfaces usually need attention every year or two, and railings and vertical parts last longer. When water stops beading on the boards, it is time.
For a deeper look at stain selection, maintenance cycles, and fences, see our Florida deck and fence staining guide and the article on treating sun-damaged wood fences.

Probing boards and doing a careful wash and stain on a ground-level deck is a fair DIY project. Hire help when structural members are soft, when the deck is elevated, or when you simply want the cleaning, drying, and staining done on the right weather window. If you hire out, ask what happens to soft boards found during prep and how the crew decides the wood is dry enough to stain. faqs.q: Can I stain over rotted deck boards?
faqs.a: No. Stain does not stop active decay, and the board will keep softening underneath. Replace rotted boards first, treat cut ends, then clean and stain the deck.
It resists rot but can still decay, especially at untreated cut ends, around fasteners, and where it stays wet. Treating cut ends and keeping the wood dry makes a big difference.

faqs.q: How often should a Florida deck be stained?
faqs.a: Horizontal boards in full sun commonly need it every one to two years. A simple test is to sprinkle water on the boards; if it soaks in instead of beading, it is time.

faqs.q: Is a rotted ledger board dangerous?
faqs.a: Yes. The ledger carries the deck where it attaches to the house. Softness or staining there should be inspected by a qualified deck builder before the deck is used heavily.
